title: Ashcroft v. Iqbal (2009)
summary: The allegations did not plausibly show that the two senior federal officials adopted the challenged detention policy for a prohibited discriminatory purpose.
notes:
The ruling did not find the alleged abuses false and did not adjudicate every claim against every defendant. Keep the parties, required mental state, pleading posture, and possibility of amendment distinct.

Justice Kennedy wrote for a 5-4 Court; the defendants were Attorney General Ashcroft and FBI Director Mueller, the case reached the Court on interlocutory appeal from the denial of qualified immunity, and the opinion sets out the two-step method: disregard conclusory allegations not entitled to the assumption of truth, then ask whether the remaining well-pleaded facts plausibly (not merely possibly) give rise to an entitlement to relief.

sections.Parties: Iqbal, a Pakistani Muslim detained after the September 11 attacks, sued federal officials, including Attorney General Ashcroft and FBI Director Mueller.
sections.Material Facts: Iqbal alleged harsh treatment and restrictive confinement while detained in a high-security unit. His allegations against the two senior officials included assertions that they designed or approved discriminatory policies. He also described a policy of holding designated detainees under restrictive conditions until cleared. The Court considered the context of the post-attack investigation in deciding whether the pleaded facts supported an inference of intentional discrimination by those particular officials.
sections.Procedural History: The district court denied the senior officials’ motion to dismiss, and the Second Circuit allowed the claims to proceed. The Supreme Court reversed and remanded; it left further consideration of amendment to the lower courts.
sections.Issue: Did the complaint plausibly allege that Ashcroft and Mueller, through their own actions, violated the plaintiff’s rights by adopting the policy for a discriminatory purpose?
sections.Holding: No. The general assertions of unconstitutional purpose were conclusory, and the remaining allegations did not plausibly establish the required discriminatory intent by these defendants.
sections.Reasoning: The Court described two connected tasks. A court first identifies allegations that merely recite elements or legal conclusions and therefore do not receive the assumption of truth. It then accepts the well-pleaded facts and asks whether they plausibly establish entitlement to relief, using the context and judicial experience. The majority considered the facts consistent with an investigation aimed at a particular security threat and found insufficient additional support for the prohibited purpose attributed to the officials. It also rejected supervisory liability based solely on office or responsibility for subordinates. The opinion applied Rule 8’s plausibility requirement beyond antitrust, and held that a deficient complaint could not be repaired simply by promising careful discovery.

learning.why: The allegations did not plausibly show that the two senior federal officials adopted the challenged detention policy for a prohibited discriminatory purpose.

topics.cp-plausibility: The Court separated conclusory assertions of discriminatory policy from factual allegations and then assessed the latter in context. The claim required allegations of each official’s own prohibited purpose, rather than supervisory status alone.
topics.cp-pleading-proof: The question concerned the sufficiency of allegations against each senior official, not a factual determination that mistreatment never occurred.
topics.cp-access: The majority required a sufficient complaint before discovery against the officials.
topics.cp-frcp-8: Iqbal applies Rule 8(a)(2) to all civil actions and explains which allegations get the assumption of truth.
topics.cp-frcp-12: The case sets the standard for deciding a Rule 12(b)(6) motion after Twombly.

learning.separateOpinions: Justice Souter’s dissent, joined by three Justices, read the allegations together and disputed both the majority’s treatment of the officials’ position on liability and its classification of the factual assertions. Justice Breyer separately emphasized judicial tools for managing discovery.

mnemonic.rationale: A detainee and the Attorney General
